source.pc: In this skill you learn to expand brackets for a power of a sum. If you see an expression like you can turn this into . This includes setting up the right format, taking powers of each of the terms, looking up the right multiplication coefficients, and eventually simplifying all individual terms. This skill only considers sums with two terms, not dealing with expansions like or similar. It also does not consider negative powers.

First we will examine the long method of expanding the brackets. We usually would not use this method in practice because we'll get very big expressions. We will still do so here anyway, just to show you what it entails. So bear with us. We will make it easier later.

The outcome may seem confusing and overly large. However, there is a reason why it is set up the way it is. To grasp this, it helps to visualize it. In geometry, a square or second power like calculates an area.
The square represents the entire area, but we can also split it up into smaller areas. If we expand brackets, then we get the expression . Here every term represents a smaller area.
We can do the same for a cube/third power like which represents a volume.

Here represents the full volume of the cube, but we can also split it up into smaller blocks. These blocks represent the individual terms in . Specifically, we have one large cube for , three square-like blocks for , three rectangular blocks for , and one small cube for .
The above method is a lot of work, and even more so when the exponent becomes bigger. So let's study a short-cut.

First we want to find the terms that will appear in the final expansion. Effectively, these are the blocks from the above cube. These areNote that we take a power of the first term and a power of the second term , making sure that both exponents add up to (the exponent we originally started off with), and subsequently multiply these two powers.

Next, we want to determine how often each of these terms will appear in the final expansion. So effectively how often each block appears in the cube. For our example, the terms appeared respectively, one, three, three and one time(s). These numbers may seem familiar if you're familiar with Pascal's triangle. Pascal's triangle is a triangle of numbers where every number is the sum of the two numbers diagonally above it.

Note row number three. It is exactly the number of times that each of our terms appeared in the final result! So if we want to know how many times a certain term appears in the final result, we look up the row corresponding to the original exponent (for us ) from Pascal's triangle.

We use the numbers from Pascal's triangle as multiplication factors for each of our terms. If we do so for our example, we get the termsFinally we add up all the resulting terms. This gives us the final resultSo the key is to first calculate the terms that will appear in the final expansion, find out how often they occur using Pascal's triangle, and then assemble the final result accordingly. Especially when the power gets big, this method will save you a lot of work compared to the alternative of expanding every individual set of brackets.
